candidates.source_body_excerpt: Seventeen people have been arrested as police tackle a “spider web of criminality” in Heywood and Rochdale. This morning, 250 officers carried out a series of raids as part of Operation Rivercrest which is targeting an organised crime group. The operation led to the execution of 20 warrants – mostly in Rochdale and Heywood – as well as in areas across Bury, Salford, Manchester, Merseyside and Yorkshire. Those arrested range in age from 19 to 49. Sixteen men have been arrested on suspicion of various offences, including drugs supply, assault, violent disorder, affray, burglary, and robbery. One woman, aged 21, was arrested on suspicion of being concerned in the supply of drugs. DS Hannah Taala, of Greater Manchester Police’s Rochdale Division, said officers focused on the crime group after violence in Heywood earlier in the year . She said: “There was a large disorder in April, where multiple people were involved in violence in the Heywood area. “It ended in some quiet serious injuries, assaults, a stab wound, using vehicles in that disorder, weapons, machetes. A cannabis farm was discovered during the raids. Image: GMP

Electricity North West said that the loss of power was linked to 'third-party interference' on the network in Newhey . A 'loud bang' could be heard when the power was lost, it was said. Some residents were left without power for about three hours. Click here to get the biggest stories straight to your inbox in our Daily Newsletter In a message to residents seen by the Manchester Evening News , Electricity North West said: "Our investigations identified that the fault was linked to third-party interference on our high-voltage network. "As a result, this customer will remain off supply while further investigations are carried out and it is confirmed safe to restore their power. "For everyone else, we were able to restore at 23:17pm once checks were completed. "We appreciate your patience and understanding while we conducted investigations on what the root cause was."

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Jordan Gibson netted twice as unbeaten Crewe registered a third consecutive victory with a 3-2 success over Rochdale. Matus Holicek fired the Alex ahead with a stunning strike before Gibson scored either side of the interval. A Joel Tabiner own goal and a late header from Aden Flint saw Dale cut the arrears, but the visitors went down to their first league defeat in six games. Crewe struck twice inside six minutes with first Holicek picking the ball up from Gibson and unleashing a drive from outside the box, which goalkeeper Sam Waller got a hand to, after 39 minutes. Young Chelsea loanee Kaiden Wilson was then brushed aside too easily by Owen Lunt and the midfielder squared the ball across the box for Gibson to tap in on the stroke of half-time before the latter poked in from 10 yards 10 minutes into the second half. Dale cut the arrears when Glenn Middleton's cross diverted off Tabiner in the 65th minute and Flint headed in substitute Ed Francis' cross from close range in the closing stages. candidates.source_body_excerpt: The battle for Hopwood Hall returns to the courtroom today with ownership of the historic manor house at stake. Hopwood DePree and Rochdale Council begin a two-day trial in the High Court in Manchester later over Mr DePree’s bid to restore his ancestral home. Mr DePree is a descendant of the Hopwood family which build the manor house in the 1420s. The family owned the hall and surrounding land — which is now Hopwood Hall College — until 1922. The house was sold 20 years later. It was occupied by a variety of temporary residents, including the de la Salle Brothers, who ran it as a Catholic teacher training college until the 1980s. It had fallen into disrepair and was bought by Rochdale Council, which still owns the Grade II-listed property. The legal action initiated by Mr DePree was launched after he spent seven years working with the council to carry out vital repairs on the dilapidated site with a view to purchasing it. In November, 2024, the council ended its exclusivity agreement with Mr DePree, and said it would explore other options because no “commercially viable” business model had been presented. READ MORE: Four arrests and £1m drugs seizure in Rochdale Mr DePree’s case is that the council went back on his option to purchase Hopwood Hall upon planning permission being granted in 2022. His claim is that the agreement triggers have been satisfied and the council must proceed with the ownership transfer.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Plans to improve the rail link between Rochdale and London have hit the buffers again. Today, the Office of Rail and Road announced it had rejected proposals for new train services which would have seen Lumo operate up to four additional return Rochdale-to-Euston services on weekdays and Saturdays and three services on Sundays . Among those backing calls for the extra services was Rochdale MP Paul Waugh, who called Lumo’s bid to restore six daily direct services between Rochdale and the capital a “game-changing opportunity” for the borough and the wider North West. But the ORR rejected the plans after its assessment found adding more trains to the West Coast Main Line — which also included services to Blackpool and Wrexham — would likely increase delays and cancelled trains for passengers. It said its assessment following detailed and extensive analysis is that the capacity and performance of the southern section of the West Coast Main Line has not materially changed since it rejected a similar application by Lumo last year. An external review commissioned by ORR also supported this conclusion. READ MORE: Police target crime gang’s ‘spider web of criminality’ The ORR said gaps in the current timetable need to provide important space for trains to recover when disruption occurs, minimising delays to passengers.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: A retired civil servant will be keeping extra warm this winter after winning 500 litres of heating oil. Liz Shrewsbury, who lives in a hamlet just outside Rochdale, won the prize in Craggs Energy’s Cosy Heating Club quarterly oil draw. Matus Holicek’s thumping finish and a double from Jordan Gibson was enough to stave off a second-half fightback from Dale and leave Crewe unbeaten in the first 11 games this term. Bell said: “It’s a big achievement with the club being 150 years old (in 2027) and for my players and staff to hold that record outright. “That’s what it takes to win a game in this league as Rochdale were on a run of five games unbeaten and played some good football, although I didn’t think they threatened us with that. “But when you’re 3-0 at home you do want it to be more comfortable than it was. They brought their big No 9 on (Emmanuel Dieseruvwe) and it was hard to contain them. “However, I thought there were plenty of opportunities for us to score a couple more goals which is what we have got to do. I want us to be an attacking side who play on the front foot most of the time. “Our second goal was really terrific. Owen Lunt is a beast and he floored their lad fairly to set up Jordan, which is exactly what we needed.” Crewe struck twice inside six minutes with first Holicek picking the ball up from Gibson and unleashing a drive from outside the box, which goalkeeper Sam Waller got a hand to, after 39 minutes.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Jordan Gibson netted twice as unbeaten Crewe registered a third consecutive victory with a 3-2 success over Rochdale. Matus Holicek fired the Alex ahead with a stunning strike before Gibson scored either side of the interval. A Joel Tabiner own goal and a late header from Aden Flint saw Dale cut the arrears, but the visitors went down to their first league defeat in six games. Crewe struck twice inside six minutes with first Holicek picking the ball up from Gibson and unleashing a drive from outside the box, which goalkeeper Sam Waller got a hand to, after 39 minutes. Young Chelsea loanee Kaiden Wilson was then brushed aside too easily by Owen Lunt and the midfielder squared the ball across the box for Gibson to tap in on the stroke of half-time before the latter poked in from 10 yards 10 minutes into the second half. Dale cut the arrears when Glenn Middleton’s cross diverted off Tabiner in the 65th minute and Flint headed in substitute Ed Francis’ cross from close range in the closing stages.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: After a turbulent two years of battling over Hopwood Hall, Rochdale’s council leader says the ‘cherished’ historic building will be brought back into use. Council bosses were quizzed over the future of the Middleton site following a High Court battle where the town hall prevailed against Hopwood DePree. The two day trial in Manchester Civil Justice Centre ruled that the council was not acting unlawfully when it ended an exclusivity agreement with the American filmmaker. Mr DePree entered an option agreement with the council to restore the hall back in 2017, until that agreement was ended in October 2024. Since then, Mr DePree, who claims ancestral connections with the 1400s stately home, has felt he had a legally binding agreement to purchase Hopwood Hall for £1. The High Court found that the ‘change of use’ planning approval was granted in 2022 wasn’t enough to trigger the option to purchase the hall for a ‘peppercorn fee’ – £1. In the first town hall meeting since the trial last month, council leader Neil Emmott was asked what the next steps were for the hall. Coun Emmott did not clarify a specific use for the future of the hall, but vowed to bring it back into use for the wider community. The council boss told the chamber on October 15 how his ‘door is always open’ to Hopwood DePree. Coun Emmott said if Mr DePree came back with a viable plan for the future of Hopwood Hall, the council would listen. In response to Coun Steve Potter’s question about the next steps for Hopwood Hall, Coun Emmott said: “The High Court’s judgment in relation to Hopwood Hall does not necessarily mark the end of the legal process. “Mr DePree has the right to seek permission to appeal the decision. The court has directed that any application for permission to appeal must be lodged by November 18, 2026, although there is scope for this deadline to be extended to November 28, 2026.
candidates.source_summary: After a turbulent two years of battling over Hopwood Hall, Rochdale’s council leader says the ‘cherished’ historic building will be brought back into use.
candidates.source_title: Hopwood Hall ‘will be brought back into community use’

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Is the future of the local pub in danger? That’s the fear in Littleborough where the closure of another pub has sparked outcry. A few months ago The Wheatsheaf closed down in the Rochdalian town. There is strong community interest in reopening the pub as a local asset, but a small loophole means they fear they can’t do that. When breweries or large companies that own and operate pubs sell on the building, they can include a covenant that prevents it from being re-used as a pub. This covenant is inserted into a sale to stop competitors taking the pub on the cheap, the latest town hall meeting was told. Coun Richard Jackson brought forward a motion to Rochdale council to address this very issue to reduce the continued loss of pubs in communities. The Littleborough Lakeside councillor told the chamber on October 15: “The reality is that around 50 per cent of pubs are owned by breweries or large pub companies. They have a history of damaging the industry as a whole. This often leads to tenant attrition. “We are acutely aware of pubs being closed down after numerous tenants have left the building. The point of this motion is to address the churn. “We have seen this at the former Royal Oak pub. This was sold with an anti-competition covenant.” The former Royal Oak pub was closed down in 2015 and then sold off and became a vape shop, which was later shut down by Trading Standards.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Bonfire night is set to go off with a bang in Rochdale with a week full of events on offer. Yet again the council is putting on three firework display events in Rochdale, Heywood and Middleton – completely free of charge. Just like last year, Bowlee Community Park, Queens Park Road and Cronkeyshaw Common will all be dazzled by pyrotechnics. This year Rochdale council are trialling reduced noise firework displays to make the events more accessible to all. Festivities will begin on Monday, November 2 at Bowlee Community Park in Middleton. The next day (October 3) will be Heywood’s Queen’s Park Road event followed by the Cronkeyshaw Common event in Syke on October 4. All three of the council-run events will see the bonfire lit at 7pm and fireworks starting from 7.30pm. Food and soft drinks will be available to buy. Alcohol will not be on sale, nor is anyone allowed to bring their own alcohol, fireworks, or sparklers. There will be no toilet facilities provided at any of the three council-run events. Those planning to head to one of the organised displays have been urged by the council to walk or use public transport if possible due to limited parking availability. Elsewhere in the borough there are other options available to people. Milnrow Cricket Club and Lobden Golf Club in Whitworth are both putting on firework displays on Saturday, November 7.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Plans for the 17-storey tower have prompted concerns over the Marble Arch's future A historic Manchester pub that has drawn visitors from around the world is fearing for its future amid plans for a large tower to be built nearby. The Marble Arch has been serving pints on Rochdale Road since 1888 when Queen Victoria sat on the throne and the city was rapidly industrialising. Plans by the McGoff Group to build a 17-storey tower with 153 flats next to the Grade II-listed pub have prompted concerns about the visual impact and the pub's continued existence. Manchester City Council said it accepted "some visual harm" would be caused as a result of the building going up, but would be "outweighed by the substantial public and regeneration benefits that the proposal would deliver". Councillors in Manchester have been recommended to approve the plans at a meeting on 22 October. The McGoff Group has been approached for a comment. Meanwhile, the Marble Arch has submitted a detailed objection against the plans, alongside the Victorian Society and Campaign for Real Ale.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: A court has ruled that Rochdale Council did not act unfairly in its decision not to pass ownership of Hopwood Hall to one of its descendants. Today marked the end of a two-day trial in the High Court in Manchester after Hopwood DePree took legal action against the council which ended an exclusivity agreement to sell the historic Grade II-listed hall to him. Following the decision, Mr DePree said: “This is of course incredibly disappointing and a huge blow to our community, our supporters around the world, as well as the UK’s charitable heritage rescue groups in general. “However, please know that my team and I are already determining our legal options and next steps. “We will be watching closely to keep an eye on Rochdale Borough Council’s efforts to save Hopwood Hall for the community, and restore it to its former glory.” Mr DePree is a descendant of the Hopwood family which build the manor house in the 1420s. The family owned the hall and surrounding land — which is now Hopwood Hall College — until 1922. The house was sold 20 years later. It was occupied by a variety of temporary residents, including the de la Salle Brothers, who ran it as a Catholic teacher training college until the 1980s. candidates.source_body_excerpt: This week's column with Councillor Neil Emmott It's been a busy and productive few weeks across our borough, with positive news, exciting regeneration projects and innovative services making a real difference for residents in Heywood, Middleton, the Pennines, and Rochdale. Since 2017, more than £1.6 million has been invested in Hopwood Hall by the council and Historic England, and we remain committed to funding essential repairs. Feasibility studies have been completed and options for its long-term future will be considered in due course. What is certain is that, once restored, Hopwood Hall will serve the wider Middleton community and continue to play an important role in the town's rich heritage. There has also been a significant boost for Middleton's regeneration ambitions, with a series of announcements demonstrating the momentum building behind the town's Mayoral Development Corporation. Meanwhile, plans are progressing to transform Middleton Scout Hut into a vibrant community venue offering activities and training opportunities for young people. There is more good news on the horizon, with banking and post office services set to return to Middleton town centre in the new year. This is something I have long championed and it will provide another welcome boost for the town centre. These projects form part of our wider commitment to invest in every part of the borough, creating jobs, driving economic growth and ensuring our communities thrive. At the recent Our Town, Our Future event, I saw first-hand the passion local residents, businesses and community groups have for Middleton and their determination to shape its future. The application will be determined by the council’s planning committee on Thursday due to the number of objections lodged against the proposals. Demolishing Chadwick Farm Barn would create access from Greenvale to the proposed development which includes 39 homes for market sale, split between 14 three-bed, seven four-bed and 18 five-bed, with six three and four-bedroom homes designated for social housing. A decision on the application was deferred in August due to a lack of a housing masterplan. Since then, the plans have received 311 additional responses, 304 of which objected to the development. They cite concerns regarding the premature release of the site ahead of a comprehensive housing masterplan, the inadequacy of local infrastructure, highway capacity and road safety, drainage and flooding, impacts on ecology and landscape and the effects upon the amenity of surrounding occupiers. candidates.source_body_excerpt: The Early Doors Club, known for staging successful early evening live music events in Bolton and Wigan, has launched in Rochdale thanks to funding from GMCA’s Culture Fund, part of a wider £15 million investment to bring culture and opportunity closer to home across Greater Manchester. The historic St Chad’s Church in the town centre will be the venue for a series of shows following the installation of a stage along with professional sound and lighting equipment. Last month the venue hosted an introductory show featuring Liam Fender supported by Rebecca Spooner, and next up is Nigel Clark, frontman of Britpop favourites Dodgy on Friday 23 October, supported by Grace Rose, a 19-year-old singer/songwriter from Heywood. Best known for hits like ‘Good Enough’, ‘Staying Out for the Summer’ and ‘If You’re Thinking of Me’, Nigel’s unmistakable voice and timeless songwriting made him one of the most enduring artists of the Britpop era. It will be an intimate performance in Rochdale filled with the warmth, humour and melody that define Dodgy’s music, along with stories from a career that’s seen him share stages with Oasis and Blur. The Early Doors Club is a grassroots live music initiative delivered by The Snug Coffee House, based in Atherton, Greater Manchester. St Chad’s Church in Rochdale joins a growing network of unique venues across Greater Manchester hosting shows. Event manager Ben Morgan from The Early Doors Club said: “Rochdale is a key area for our expansion, building on the work of the local cultural team to bring more events and opportunities into areas where people live and work. Rochdale Development Agency’s commitment to improving access to culture is why we want to be there and we’re excited to help build something for the town.” Since its 2023 debut The Early Doors Club has staged more than 160 events, attracted over 13,500 people and supported more than 250 artists. Nearly half of audiences have travelled from outside the host area, highlighting its role in boosting town centres and supporting local economies. The project is designed to break down barriers to live music, with performances in cafés, churches, community halls and heritage spaces on the high street. Events start early and finish by 9pm, making them accessible for those using public transport and anyone who prefers earlier evenings. Tickets are offered on a ‘pay what you can basis’, so price doesn’t prevent anyone from attending. Councillor Sue Smith, cabinet member for communities and co-operation at Rochdale Borough Council, said: “I’m pleased to see The Early Doors Club coming to Rochdale in such a beautiful venue. Live music has the power to bring people together, support our local economy and showcase the borough as a vibrant destination for culture and entertainment. These gigs will give residents the chance to enjoy fantastic professionally produced performances on their doorstep while also attracting visitors into the town centre. It’s also great to see the investment in the church as well as Rochdale’s music scene and I look forward to seeing audiences come together to support these events.”

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Renovating Rochdale’s iconic Seven Sisters tower blocks would force residents out of their homes for more than a decade, housing chiefs have said. While Rochdale Boroughwide Housing says no decision on the future of the landmark College Bank blocks has been taken, residents have asked new Greater Manchester Mayor Bev Craig to back their campaign to refurbish their homes rather than demolish them. But if campaigners get their wish, the scale of bringing the 61-year-old buildings up to modern standards would take more than 10 years and they could not be occupied until the work is complete, RBH chiefs have said. Members of Greater Manchester Tenants Union recently met Ms Craig to discuss the steps that could be taken to renovate almost 1,000 homes in College Bank and Lower Falinge. Plans to demolish College Bank were first discussed in 2017 when RBH warned that the buildings were approaching the end of their life. Tenants set up the Save the Seven Sisters campaign and hoped RBH’s partnership with Legal and General Affordable Homes would see the towers restored. But in September, 2024, it was announced that the partnership would not continue. The union and the Save the Seven Sisters campaign asked then Greater Manchester Mayor Andy Burnham to help. In November, 2024, the Mayoral Taskforce was established to look at the options for the College Bank estate. Rochdale’s skyline without the Seven Sisters towers. Image: Copilot In October 2025, RBH announced the results of surveys which found the blocks were not safe to remain occupied and residents would be required to leave their homes.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Developers want to build 450 houses on former playing fields in Rochdale . The fate of one of the initial phases of the giant scheme will be decided next week. In August, Rochdale council ’s planning committee delayed making a decision on Wain Home’s plan to build 45 houses on a plot of land behind Greenvale, in Bamford. The committee felt they didn’t have enough detail about drainage from the developers. The site, to the west of Norden Road, has a history of flooding. So the panel of councillors wanted to ensure proper precautions were being taken by the developer before making a decision. Click here to get the biggest stories straight to your inbox in our Daily Newsletter This scheme would be the first of many for the former green belt land – which contains a number of playing fields and sports pitches. The Bamford site was taken out of green belt status after the adoption of the Greater Manchester housing strategy named Places for Everyone. A new clubhouse for Bridge FC and revamped sports pitches within the site are seen as the major benefits that would come from the overarching scheme. The plan would see access created through the demolition of Chadwick Farm Barn on Greenvale. In its place a T-junction would provide vehicle access to the site. It wasn’t just flood risks that the planning committee took issue with. Objectors at the meeting on August 5 raised concern over there being no safeguarding set in stone for how transport connectivity, drainage, highways, and local amenities would work across the whole site. To get the very latest from Manchester's political scene in your newsfeed - click here to add the MEN as your preferred Google source Planning agent Gareth Salthouse, representing Wain Homes, explained that drainage for the site had been assessed and said this plan could be done quickly to bring ‘much-needed housing’ to the area. The planning committee was also concerned about the lack of overall masterplan. Coun Tom Besford feared this ‘piecemeal development’ would see each developer do the bare minimum of affordable homes for each plot on the land. He felt this would eventually result in all the benefits not coming to fruition. Coun Besford said: “Why would we go through the blood, sweat and tears of getting PfE over the line but then just give this land away. We have to assume that we could get 10 other plans like this. “Then what if it doesn’t add up and everything falls short overall.” The committee agreed to defer the decision based on questions over drainage. They will reconvene on Thursday, October 22 to make a final decision on the scheme.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: People are being urged to remain vigilant following several reports of calls involving scammers impersonating police officers to obtain personal and sensitive information linked to cryptocurrency. Greater Manchester Police said one common method is to claim that they have arrested a suspect who was in possession of the victim’s personal documents, such as their passport, driving licence or banking details. On several occasions, fraudsters asked victims about their cryptocurrency accounts, specifically looking for their IDs, recovery phrases, and security codes. GMP says officers will never ask anyone to share this information or move your accounts. Police say the calls can appear convincing and are being made through spoofed GMP phone numbers. DS Reed, of GMP Cyber Crime Team, said: “These calls are an incredibly sophisticated type of crime, and those responsible are targeting our vulnerable communities. “We take offences of this nature incredibly seriously, and our team is working around the clock to understand how these offences have occurred, and how to prevent it from continuing. “Our officers will never get you to share security codes or personal information in relation to cryptocurrency, and if you are receiving calls that ask you to do so, please do not respond and report to us immediately.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: A major milestone has been reached for Atom Valley with completion of the base build of the Sustainable Materials & Manufacturing Centre (SMMC) at Kingsway Business Park in Rochdale, which is set to become a nationally significant gateway driving the development of the advanced materials and manufacturing cluster in the region. The 30,000 sq. ft centre is the first major physical development within the Atom Valley Innovation District (AVID), a 25-acre hub for advanced materials and manufacturing in Rochdale, bringing together businesses, researchers, investors and innovation partners in one location. AVID provides an environment where organisations can innovate, grow and commercialise new technologies, strengthening Greater Manchester’s position as a leading centre for advanced materials and manufacturing. Completion of the building represents a major milestone for years of partnership working between Rochdale Development Agency (RDA), Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA), The University of Manchester and wider innovation partners. RDA has led the physical development of the SMMC, working with partners to secure investment and position advanced materials and manufacturing as a priority opportunity for Rochdale and Greater Manchester. The next phase will see work move from construction towards specialist fit-out ahead of bringing the centre into operation in 2027. The RDA brought together partners from industry, academia and government to establish the Centre of Expertise in Advanced Materials and Sustainability (CEAMS) in 2023. Since then, businesses have been able to connect with a national network of specialist expertise, facilities and innovation support through the CEAMS partners, including The University of Manchester, the Henry Royce Institute, National Physical Laboratory (NPL), Centre for Process Innovation (CPI) and NCC (formerly National Composites Centre). CEAMS has already supported more than 90 companies, developing new products and processes and demonstrating the value of a more connected innovation ecosystem.
